title: Old Phones, New Treasure: Recycling Electronics
summary: Why old phones and other electronics hold valuable metals, how e-waste can harm the land when it is thrown away, how devices are recycled, and what students can do to help.
poll: An old phone in a drawer is just junk.

versions.title: Old Phones Are Not Junk
versions.text:
Do you have an old phone in a box? It is not junk. It holds a treasure!

A phone has bits of metal in it. Some is gold. Some is silver. Some is copper. They are hard to find.

We throw out lots of old phones. This is e-waste. Most of it is just thrown out. What a waste!

Old phones in the trash hurt the land. Bad stuff can leak out. It gets in the dirt. It gets in the water. A battery in the trash can start a fire.

We can recycle old phones. People take them apart. They sort the parts. They melt the metal. Then they make new things with it.

We dig mines to get new metal. Mines hurt the land. Old phones hold more gold than the same heap of rock from a mine! So it is best to recycle.

What can you do? Keep your phone a long time. Fix it. Give it to a friend. Or take it to a drop box. Wipe it first.

Saudi Arabia wants us to recycle more. You can help.

versions.title: Treasure in Old Phones
versions.text:
Is there an old phone in a drawer at home? It may look like junk. But it holds a hidden treasure!

A phone has small bits of metal in it. Some of it is gold. Some is silver, and some is copper. These metals are hard to find.

Each year, the world throws out a huge pile of old phones and TVs. We call this e-waste. Most of it is not used again. That is a big waste!

Old phones in the trash can hurt the land. Bad stuff inside them can leak out. It gets into the soil and water. A battery in the trash can even start a fire.

But we can recycle old phones. Workers take them apart. They sort the parts. They melt the metal. Then it is used to make new things.

To get new metal, people dig big mines. Mines can harm the land. A heap of old phones holds more gold than the same heap of rock from a mine! It is much better to recycle.

What can you do? Keep your phone for a long time. Fix it if it breaks. Give it to a friend who needs it. Or take it to a drop-off point. Delete your photos first!

Saudi Arabia has a plan to recycle much more. You can help, too.

Is there an old phone sitting in a drawer at your home? It may look like junk, but inside that small case is a hidden treasure.

Every phone contains tiny amounts of valuable metals. There is a little gold, some silver, and some copper. Its battery holds other metals, too. These materials are hard to find in nature, and some of them are also rare.

Each year, people around the world throw away millions of tons of old electronic devices, such as phones, laptops, and TVs. This is called e-waste. Less than a quarter of it is collected and recycled. The rest is wasted.

When old electronics are thrown into a landfill, they can be harmful. Some contain lead or mercury, which can leak into the soil and water. A battery thrown in the trash can even catch fire inside a garbage truck.

The good news is that old devices can be recycled. First, they are collected. Next, workers take them apart and sort the pieces. Then the metals are separated, melted down, and cleaned. Finally, they are used again to make new products.

To get new metal, people must dig huge mines. Mining can damage the land and use a lot of energy. In fact, a ton of old phones contains more gold than a ton of rock from a gold mine. Recycling saves metal and protects nature.

What can you do? Keep your phone as long as you can, and repair it when it breaks. Give it to someone who needs it, or take it to a collection point. Just remember to delete your photos and messages first.

Saudi Arabia has set goals to recycle much more of its waste and send less to landfills. Every phone you recycle helps.

versions.title: Old Phones, New Treasure: Recycling Electronics
versions.text:
Is there perhaps an obsolete phone currently languishing, forgotten, within a drawer somewhere in your home? It may superficially resemble useless junk, but concealed inside that unassuming plastic casing lies a hidden treasure that most people never seriously pause to consider.

Every phone contains minute quantities of genuinely valuable metals, including small amounts of gold, silver, and copper. Its rechargeable battery incorporates additional useful metallic elements. These particular materials prove difficult and expensive to extract directly from nature through conventional mining. Several of them are relatively scarce globally, which renders each one a precious resource thoroughly deserving of careful conservation rather than careless disposal.

Each year, people distributed across the entire world discard millions of tons of obsolete electronic devices, encompassing phones, laptops, and televisions alike. This particular category of discarded material is formally designated electronic waste, or e-waste for short. Less than a quarter of this material is collected and recycled appropriately through proper channels. This consequently means that the overwhelming majority of these valuable materials become permanently and irretrievably lost.

When individuals dispose of electronics carelessly, the discarded devices frequently accumulate within landfills, where they can gradually become genuinely hazardous to the surrounding natural environment. Certain devices contain toxic substances such as lead or mercury, which can slowly seep into the underlying soil and subsequently contaminate groundwater supplies. A discarded lithium battery can even spontaneously ignite while compressed inside an ordinary garbage truck.

Fortunately, obsolete devices can be successfully recycled through a meticulously designed, multi-stage industrial process. Initially, devices are collected and transported to a specialized recycling facility, where trained technicians dismantle them carefully and systematically categorize the various internal components. Subsequently, the recovered metals are separated, melted down, and chemically purified. This enables manufacturers to incorporate them directly into newly manufactured electronic devices.

To obtain equivalent quantities of brand-new metal through conventional means, mining corporations must excavate truly enormous pits within the earth. These operations can devastate the surrounding landscape and consume a tremendous quantity of energy in the process. Remarkably, a single ton of discarded phones contains considerably more recoverable gold than an equivalent ton of raw rock extracted from an active gold mine. This renders recycling a genuinely sustainable alternative for supplying the increasingly scarce metals that contemporary technology fundamentally requires.

What practical action can you personally take? Preserve your phone for as long as reasonably possible, and repair it promptly whenever it malfunctions rather than immediately replacing it with a new device. Donate it to someone who genuinely needs it, or deliver it conscientiously to an official collection point, although remember to delete all personal information thoroughly beforehand.

Saudi Arabia has established ambitious national objectives to recycle substantially more of its generated waste while sending considerably less material to landfills. Every single phone that you personally recycle contributes meaningfully to the Kingdom's broader environmental progress and sustainability goals.

versions.title: Old Phones, New Treasure: Recycling Electronics
versions.text:
Is there perhaps an obsolete phone currently languishing, entirely forgotten, within some drawer in your home at this very moment? It may superficially resemble nothing more than useless junk, but concealed inside that unassuming plastic casing lies a genuinely hidden treasure that most people never seriously pause to consider or appreciate.

Every single phone contains minute, almost imperceptible quantities of genuinely valuable metals, including small amounts of gold, silver, and copper, while its accompanying rechargeable battery additionally incorporates further useful metallic elements of commercial value. These particular raw materials prove consistently difficult and prohibitively expensive to extract directly from the natural environment through conventional mining operations, and several among them are relatively scarce on a global scale, which collectively renders each one a genuinely precious resource thoroughly deserving of careful, deliberate conservation rather than careless, thoughtless disposal.

Each successive year, people distributed across the entire globe discard millions upon millions of tons of obsolete electronic devices, encompassing phones, laptops, and televisions alike, and this particular category of discarded material is formally designated electronic waste, or e-waste for short, within environmental and industrial contexts. Less than a quarter of this considerable material is collected and recycled appropriately through proper, regulated channels, which consequently means that the overwhelming majority of these valuable constituent materials become permanently and quite irretrievably lost to productive use.

When individuals dispose of their electronics carelessly and without forethought, the discarded devices frequently accumulate within sprawling landfills, where they can gradually become genuinely hazardous to the surrounding natural environment over extended periods. Certain devices contain demonstrably toxic substances such as lead or mercury, which can slowly seep through the soil and subsequently contaminate underlying groundwater supplies relied upon by nearby communities, and a carelessly discarded lithium battery can even spontaneously ignite while compressed inside an ordinary municipal garbage truck.

Fortunately, obsolete devices can nevertheless be successfully recycled through a meticulously designed, multi-stage industrial process requiring considerable technical expertise. Initially, devices are collected systematically and transported to a specialized recycling facility, where trained technicians dismantle them with care and methodically categorize the numerous internal components by material type. Subsequently, the recovered metals are carefully separated, melted down under controlled conditions, and chemically purified, thereby enabling manufacturers to incorporate them directly into the construction of newly manufactured electronic devices.

To obtain equivalent quantities of brand-new metal through entirely conventional means, mining corporations must excavate truly enormous pits within the earth's crust, operations that can devastate the surrounding natural landscape irreversibly and consume a genuinely tremendous quantity of energy throughout the extraction process. Remarkably, a single ton of discarded phones contains considerably more recoverable gold than an equivalent ton of raw rock extracted directly from an active, operating gold mine, a comparison which renders recycling an unambiguously sustainable alternative for supplying the increasingly scarce metallic resources that contemporary digital technology fundamentally requires for continued production.

What practical, concrete action might you personally undertake? Preserve your phone in working order for as long as reasonably possible, and repair it promptly whenever it malfunctions rather than immediately replacing it wholesale with an entirely new device. Donate it generously to someone who genuinely needs it, or deliver it conscientiously to an official, designated collection point, although remember always to delete all personal information thoroughly and completely beforehand.

Saudi Arabia has established genuinely ambitious national objectives aimed at recycling substantially more of its generated waste while simultaneously sending considerably less material to landfills across the Kingdom, and every single phone that you personally choose to recycle contributes meaningfully to this broader national environmental progress and long-term sustainability agenda.

MID.prompt: Explain the steps that turn an old phone into material for new products. Then tell why these steps are better than throwing the phone away.
checklist: I explained the recycling steps in order.
I gave at least one reason recycling is better than throwing away.
I used key words such as electronic, valuable, and landfill.
MID.modelAnswer: First, old electronic devices are collected and taken to a special factory. Next, workers take them apart and sort the pieces, and then the metals are separated, melted down, and cleaned so they can be used again. This is better than throwing the phone away, because electronics dumped in a landfill can leak harmful lead or mercury into the soil and water, while recycling saves the valuable metals inside instead of wasting them.

keyWords.definition: poisonous and able to harm living things

keyWords.definition: to get rid of something, usually by throwing it away

keyWords.definition: able to continue for a long time without using up or harming nature

HIGH.prompt: The article calls recycling a sustainable alternative to mining. Do you agree? Explain your opinion using at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
checklist: I used at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I explained how each piece of evidence supports my opinion.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I agree that recycling is a sustainable alternative to mining, because the article shows how much it can save compared with digging new resources out of the ground. For example, a ton of old phones contains much more gold than a ton of rock from a gold mine, so recycling can extract more valuable metal with far less digging. In addition, mining new metal requires huge mines that damage the land and use a great deal of energy, while recycling simply reuses metals that already exist instead of harming more of the environment. Because recycling gets more value from materials we already have and avoids some of mining's toxic and destructive effects, it truly is a more sustainable choice.
